Recently discovered GaCu3(OH)6Cl2 has been highlighted as a unique material that combines the study of Dirac electrons with many-body physics. It exhibits significant interlayer ferromagnetic ordering along the c-axis and large intralayer antiferromagnetic frustration. By combining high-quality single-crystal samples with resonant X-ray scattering measurements, the underlying atomic-scale mechanism of its electronic and magnetic properties has been unveiled. The material's structure consists of two types of layers: metallic Cu2+ oxide triangular layers and insulating Ga1+ chloride van der Waals layers. The charge transfer from the oxide to the chloride layers results in an odd number of electrons in the Ga1+Cl2- layers, leading to an emergent atomic-scale electric dipole moment. The charge transfer also causes the electrons in the Ga1+Cl2- layers to be in a high-spin state, which mediates the unusual double-exchange interaction that causes the long-range ferromagnetic ordering. The insulating nature of the Ga1+Cl2- layers prevents the screening of the large intralayer antiferromagnetic frustration in the Cu2+ oxide triangular layers, ultimately resulting in the multiferroic properties of GaCu3(OH)6Cl2.

To address the issue of fitting bimodal data with a distribution, this study develops a new bimodal beta distribution called the Bimodal Beta-2 (Bibeta-2). By utilizing two separate beta distributions focused on different modes, Bibeta-2 offers a more efficient and straightforward approach, unlike other existing bimodal beta distributions that require complex conditions or parameters to achieve a bimodal effect. Furthermore, this study explores estimating Bibeta-2 parameters through the Maximum Likelihood Method and provides a table of maximum likelihood values and corresponding standard errors for various data sets.

The search for a second type of heavy neutral lepton is being conducted by analyzing electron + missing transverse momentum data from the CMS detector at the LHC, during runs 13 and 13.6 TeV with 35.9 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity. The analysis focuses on decays of the second Higgs boson sneutrino with a mass below 640 GeV into either a pair of opposite-charged electrons or an electron paired with a muon. The obtained limits on the branching fraction, being less than 0.47 at a 95% confidence level for a 300 GeV sneutrino, are constrained by the electron channel alone due to the high sensitivity of the relevant exclusion region. The analysis yields limits on the absolute cross section times branching fraction, being most stringent for masses above 350 GeV. Given the current search sensitivity, the CMS detector is capable of improving the limits by a factor of 1.5 to 3 with 35 fb^-1 of additional data. The electron channel alone is expected to be able to impose limits up to 500 GeV with a 3000 fb^-1 integrated luminosity. The electron + muon channel alone is capable of imposing limits up to 650 GeV with 3000 fb^-1 integrated luminosity.

In this paper, we revisit the counterpropagating beams' relationship in a closed loop, which is fundamental to Sagnac interferometry, particularly the implications of longitudinal Doppler shift. Our analysis demonstrates that a simple application of special relativity reveals the beams experience different phase shifts due to this phenomenon, counteracting each other and nullifying the effects on the counterpropagating phase, thereby preserving the phase difference used in Sagnac interferometry.

In contrast to the well-known fact that a nilfibre cannot have a dense orbit under a group action that's solvably extendable, our work demonstrates that a nilfibre can contain a dense orbit for a subgroup subgroup, and specifically, it can be the case where this subgroup is not closed. This result is exemplified through a specific construction, namely the space $n$-jet of a parabolic manifold which has a dense orbit of a specific subgroup, which in turn is not closed.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of powerful language models capable of tasks like machine translation and summarization. Despite these achievements, a key challenge remains in effectively using language models for generative tasks due to their inability to directly control generation and their tendency to produce repetitive outputs. To address this, our research proposes an approach that integrates language models, specifically $N$-gram models and neural language models, to enhance performance. By incorporating external references and a unique score calculation method, our approach enables controlled generation and diverse output probabilities. Through automatic evaluation metrics and human judgments, our strategy demonstrates superior results, particularly with shorter gram sizes, outperforming baseline models in the meantime.

This study introduces two new invariants for the linked equivalence classes of Laurent polynomials, specifically in relation to their singularities and geometric properties of Fano varieties. When applied to a Laurent polynomial defined on a torus within an algebraic variety that can be extended to a closed variety within a larger torus variety, specific properties of the polynomial are found to be equivalent to those of the underlying variety. Consequently, the primary mutation classes of Laurent polynomials, a combination of its singularity class and codimension of its singularities, are discovered to be an integral and integral-preserving property of the closed variety. Furthermore, the concept of integral motion is redefined and found to be more extensive than traditional integral motion.

Recently, generating a 3D face from 2D images has become a popular topic in computer vision research. The primary objective is to create a 3D face that accurately reflects the input 2D image in terms of shape and appearance. Existing approaches can be broadly classified into two categories: one that treats the input image as a single source and the other that regards it as a composite of pose-dependent and pose-independent latent factors. In this research, we propose a novel framework called Self-aligned Dual face Reconstruction Network (SADRNet) that addresses face reconstruction from a single input image by treating it as a combination of pose-dependent and pose-independent latent factors. The SADRNet framework employs an innovative factor-separation strategy that aligns the pose-dependent and pose-independent factors with each other and the input image. To facilitate this alignment, we introduce an auxiliary factor alignment loss function. The proposed SADRNet framework is evaluated on the widely-used Face Synchronization Dataset (FSD) and AR datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

We reexamine the mobility of fractional charges within Z_p gauge theories defined on a cubic lattice in three dimensions, utilizing an exact analytical approach through the Lehmann representation and Monte Carlo simulations of the appropriate Matsubara Green's function. Our analysis of the short-distance expansion of the mobility tensor in the large momentum regime reveals that the mobility is dominated by the charge's velocity and its mass tensor, with the mass tensor's eigenvalues exhibiting a specific power-law increase with the charge density. This expansion provides a theoretical basis for the observed results of numerical simulations. Furthermore, we investigate the mobility in one-dimensional systems with explicit exact solutions and also with numerical accuracy on par with the Lehmann representation. Here the mobility displays unique behavior that deviates from its three-dimensional counterpart.

We investigate the standard scenario of slow-roll inflation, analyzing the production of particles during the roll phase, primarily in the context of $R^2$ gravity and a minimally coupled scalar field, and examine the implications for the Bardeen potential's spectrum. The calculation of the scalar spectrum is directly linked to the number of particles created, and we find that a significant excess of particles in the $R^2$ gravity model leads to the creation of gravity waves, detectable through the $f_NL$ parameter. Moreover, we find that the calculation of the Bardeen potential's spectrum is consistent with observations of the CMBR in the standard model of slow-roll inflation, and that the interaction between the inflaton and $R^2$ term may have a lasting effect on the power spectrum of the Bardeen potential.

This work is centered on the varied forms of marked ordered trees, which are derived from standard ordered trees by designating one or more nodes as 'marked'. Initially, we explore and identify several types of marked ordered trees, including a newly defined variant. Subsequently, we employ these tree variations to derive matched parentheses expressions in a marked manner. Notably, in our work the average number of deeply nested parentheses in standard ordered trees equates to 2, whereas in marked ordered trees with at least $k$ marked nodes it equals $\pi(k)$, an increasing function of $k$.

Historically, elections have been secured through various methods such as trusted individuals, simple majority displays, basic tabulation, and complex optical character recognition systems. Our research focuses on character recognition-based vote counting by integrating a sophisticated spell-checking algorithm. We developed a customized BERT-based BERT-ADAM for enhanced character recognition, subsequently scaling the scoring to reflect a character's frequency within specific precincts and districts. Our adaptive BERT-ADAM algorithm demonstrated superior performance compared to the standard BERT model, and our scaled approach significantly improved character recognition accuracy. Furthermore, we designed a multi-stage BERT-ADAM filter to identify and remove erroneous votes, and assessed this method on a simulated dataset of 10,000 votes, comparing the results to hand-counted totals.

In highly parameterized models that depend on time, models dealing with an infinite amount of data are commonly used as a theoretical framework, providing a more realistic and practical approach than the standard approach of assuming model parameters do not change with time. Building on this approach, we develop a new statistical learning method for linear models that depend on time and can handle time-varying variables efficiently. Our method uses a novel technique of regularization and projection to create a model that is both highly parameterized and depends on time. We establish a new mathematical principle of convergence and demonstrate through numerical experiments that our method outperforms other methods in solving systems of differential equations and estimating models that depend on time and are given as a set of data.

This study proposes a novel end-to-end architecture for speech enhancement using bidirectional attention mechanisms. By incorporating elements from recent success, our method utilizes bidirectional attention to capture both temporal dependencies and global spectral features in cleaned speech signals. We conducted experiments on the speech enhancement task and observed significant improvements in quality, outperforming other methods including Conformer-based models. Our proposed framework is a straightforward and effective solution that can be easily extended for speech transformation.

A novel attack on next-generation privacy-presuring systems (NPPS) is presented, which exploits a vulnerability in pressure sensors used for safety monitoring. This attack leverages the DPSs that measure the system's internal pressure to guarantee its proper functioning. By exploiting the DPSs' susceptibility to manipulation, it is demonstrated how an adversary can influence the DPSs' readings and thereby deceive the safety system. Specifically, the vulnerability exploitation involves the creation of a pressure gauge that deceptively measures DPSs' output signals, thereby causing the NPPS to misinterpret the system's safety status. By NPPS' reliance on open-source components, the attack takes advantage of the systems' design flaws, which allow pressure to be applied to the system without triggering the safety mechanism. Ultimately, the research presented highlights the importance of addressing security vulnerabilities in safety-critical systems and the potential risks associated with relying on software-based privacy preservation technologies.

To achieve a low-carbon energy system, policy interventions are necessary to
encourage power plant participation in capacity markets while also promoting
the adoption of renewable energy sources. A significant barrier to this goal is
the behavior of risk-averse storage resources, which have a tendency to hoard
energy capacity during periods of scarcity. This paper presents a mathematical
model that analyzes the effects of two potential strategies to mitigate storage
resource hoarding behavior. The first strategy involves the use of a financial
instrument, such as a derivative security, to hedge against scarcity and
provide a reliable source of scarcity pricing information. The second strategy
examines the potential for a capacity market reserve price to mitigate hoarding
behavior. Our research indicates that both strategies can effectively address
the hoarding problem under certain conditions. Moreover, our model shows that
the impact of these strategies on market efficiency depends on the likelihood
of supply-demand imbalance and the value of the financial instrument's payoff.
These findings have significant implications for the design of energy policy and
highlight the importance of considering storage resource behavior when developing
market mechanisms.

By utilizing two different femtosecond x-ray pulses at specific energy levels, 
we can manipulate coherent motion of electrons in highly excited states through 
the excitation of a core. In a study on oxygen molecules, we observed the effect 
of changing the energy of a single x-ray pulse on the motion of electrons. 
Surprisingly, a small shift in x-ray energy had a large impact on the motion of 
electrons, affecting their oscillation frequency and the strength of this 
oscillation. Our findings can be used to more effectively control molecular 
states with x-ray pulses in the future and enhance our understanding of 
interactions between particles when exposed to x-rays.

A global baroclinic storm system has persisted on Mars for nearly a decade. This
system, located in the planet's north polar region, is composed of rotating weather
patterns that are similar to those found in the atmosphere of the Earth's north pole.
The stability of this system is influenced by the interaction between the planet's
rotational forces and the movement of its weather. Under optimal conditions,
this stability allows for the prediction of long-term weather changes. Our
research method, which is based on a simplified model of Mars' atmospheric dynamics,
is capable of providing such a forecast. This method can also be applied to other
planets with complex atmospheric systems. With the ability to monitor the planet's
weather patterns from space, this model of predictability can be enhanced. Our
research model is now integrated with data from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter to
improve the accuracy of long-term weather forecasts on Mars.

Most of the success stories in active learning are based on the use of large-scale datasets, such as ImageNet. Unfortunately, many commonly used evaluation methods employ smaller benchmark datasets, which can lead to misleading conclusions about the efficiency of active learning algorithms. These methods can be deceptive because the assumptions underlying active learning do not hold true for such datasets. To address this issue, we have developed a novel evaluation protocol that uses a more rigorous test. This protocol is based on a large-scale dataset and involves comparing the performance of state-of-the-art active learning algorithms against a traditional random sampling baseline. Our results show that several commonly used active learning algorithms, including those that focus on uncertainty and preference-based methods, perform worse than random sampling. This outcome highlights the need to rethink current evaluation practices and the design of future active learning algorithms.

This paper links the concept of generalized algebraic multiplicity to cyclicity using a specific operator known as the Schur operator, thereby expanding upon previous work by Rota and Gohberg, and Rota. By characterizing the generalized algebraic multiplicity through the Schur operator, a fundamental property of this operator naturally gives rise to the Jordan product.

To achieve quantum-enhanced sensing of an optical phase, our proposal leverages an existing technique in interferometric metrology, combining two-optical-phase-sensing with existing quantum-enhanced sensing for one mode. By utilizing the substantial photon-number difference between the modes in a single-photon-minus-one-photon-state, we can obtain a significant improvement in phase-sensing sensitivity, specifically the square root of the photon-number difference. This proposed method also highlights the potential for even greater gains in phase-sensing sensitivity, equivalent to the total photon-number.

Researchers have been focusing on using silicon based quantum computing, particularly with electron or hole donors, to achieve a two-qubit isotropic "molecular" gate. By employing a novel approach, we have developed a design for a molecular donor two-qubit gate in a planar configuration. In this approach, a single donor atom is placed near the two-qubit gate consisting of three donor atoms. This fourth donor atom serves as a pump, directing phase interference patterns and modifying the location and orientation of the interference from the main donor cluster. By utilizing a 2D simulation, we have found a configuration where a 0.05 GHz phaser doner can increase the zero-error tolerance of the gate to 0.25 GHz. Additionally, this phaser doner significantly enhances the zero-error tolerance of the gate in a direction perpendicular to the main doner cluster. However, introducing the extra donor also lowers the temperature stability of the wave function. Nevertheless, we have demonstrated that the proposed design can be used with a 0.2 MHz temperature variation. Furthermore, simulations show that the two types of doner can be controlled separately using an external magnetic field gradient.

We observed persistent resistance fluctuations near the lowest Landau level in substantial samples for over a month, associated with daily resistance changes of up to 10 Ohms and minor fluctuations as low as 0.1 Ohms. These observations were made in large samples, producing many identical, overlapping quantum layers in response to slowly increasing magnetic fields. Our experiments revealed that the observed fluctuations correspond to the tunneling of individual and pairs of electrons between these layers. The large electron numbers (up to 10^9) in these samples prevent the fluctuations from being affected by interactions within the levels.

This research proposes an innovative Adaptive Cooperative NOMA transmission protocol, which dynamically adjusts its strategy based on real-time information availability. The protocol灵活运用 two approaches: a traditional one with relatively low overhead, and an adaptive one that minimizes complex exchanges of information. To evaluate performance, we developed analytical formulas for the outage probability, which are both precise and easy to calculate. Our analysis reveals that the proposed protocol outperforms existing alternatives, even with limited information exchange, by optimizing cooperative coverage without requiring overhead increases. Furthermore, we developed a performance assessment model to analyze the trade-offs between overhead and performance, which demonstrates the protocol's superiority in terms of information exchange.

In rapidly changing TDD networks, efficiently distributing power and scheduling users is crucial, especially when some uplink transmissions may interfere with neighboring downlink receptions. To tackle this challenge, we developed a dynamic power allocation scheme using Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) to minimize the sum mean outage probability while accounting for stochastic interference and finite power constraints. A Q-learning algorithm was utilized to achieve this goal, and its performance was analyzed through simulation, comparing it to an ideal solution and a greedy power allocation method. Additionally, a scheme was proposed to reduce computational complexity by partitioning the set of affected base stations into distinct groups. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed solution significantly outperforms the greedy method and approaches the performance of the ideal solution.

A theory has been proposed to explain how vortex lines interact within a superfluid, specifically focusing on the activation energies of defects, both in isolation and in pairs. To validate this, we used direct numerical simulations to test our hypothesis and found a activation energy value for a single vortex activation ($\epsilon_a$) and a more high activation energy value for a vortex-anti-vortex pair ($\epsilon_a^*$). Notably, $\epsilon_a^*$ is about 1.5 times greater than $\epsilon_a$. Our findings also show that the energy values align with predictions made by the Kelvin wave model, with the single vortex activation following an $e^{-\epsilon_a/E_\kappa}$ pattern, and the anti-Planckian ratio $E_\kappa/\kappa \approx 0.54$.

A new numerical method has been developed to compute normalized cumulmites of the partition function for the 2D Ising model under a non-zero magnetic field. Using this method, specific values for fourth and sixth normalized cummulates were obtained on different lattice sizes, including a 2x2 lattice and infinite 1D Ising chains in a non-zero magnetic field. The results show that a phase transition can be detected through the behavior of normalized cumulmutes at a critical temperature, particularly where the 4th normalized cummulate equals -1 and the 6th normalized cummulate equals 1 at a non-zero magnetic field. The phase transition point can be identified as the temperature where the 4th and 6th normalized cummulate curves intersect, particularly on a 2x2 lattice with specific values for beta and the external field h. Furthermore, the normalized cummulate values approach these limits on larger lattice sizes when the external field is not zero.

In 2D topological systems, product states of weak interaction perturbations can reveal information about topological order when specific criteria are met. A set of sufficient conditions was established to ensure that topological properties are preserved. Utilizing the language of tensor networks, this approach allows for the computation of string order parameters via projection techniques. A key outcome of this research is the identification of a class of entanglement measures - multi-point functions defined on circular geometries - that are directly related to another set of complex mathematical objects known as 4-tensors. Notably, certain 4-tensors exhibit characteristics that facilitate analysis in the context of the toric code and the Fibonacci Hamiltonian, making them more accessible for further study.

A Hamiltonian Neural Network, capable of modeling complex dynamics, including those found in the MNIST dataset, demonstrates superior performance to an approximately 10 times larger LSTM-based meta-learner when teaching robots to generalize from just a single demonstration of grasping an object.

Our research centers on a cutting-edge concept in federated learning, where multiple agents collaborate to enhance a machine learning model's performance, simultaneously improving accuracy and trust. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel multi-agent framework inspired by reinforcement learning and Fictitious Self-Play, which enables agents to optimize a score balancing accuracy and trust through a collaborative process. Through our experiments using a simulation, our agent system outperformed a competitive method in federated learning, achieving superior results in both accuracy and trust score. Additionally, our approach shows robustness against malicious clients who submit fraudulent data, effectively resisting their attacks and producing trustworthy predictions.

This comprehensive dataset consists of 14,794 X-ray images, featuring concealed concealed items in laptop bags, backpacks, and briefcases in a variety of settings. To ensure the robustness of detection and classification algorithms, these rules have been carefully tested and validated. To facilitate the development of prohibited items security algorithms, this paper describes the creation of HiXray and presents several baseline methods for solving related tasks. In recent years, a specific polynomial family has been shown to generate an invariant for oriented links and tangles when combined with a rational function as weights. It has been found that this combination yields a non-trivial invariant for oriented links precisely when the polynomial family is the $I_3$ variant. The rational function's coefficients are given non-zero weights to the oriented link's edges, and these weights are preserved by the resulting invariant. The combination of the polynomial $J_n^R$ from the $I_3$ family and a rational function $R$ results in a map from the oriented virtual braid group to a specific rational function field, which is surjective for a sufficient number of elements. The number needed is equal to the number of elements in the oriented virtual braid group minus the number of rational points at which the function $P$ is evaluated.

Recent advancements in deep learning for NLP have been fueled by massive, easily obtainable datasets. However, as these resources dwindle, there's a pressing need for effective data augmentation techniques that can enhance performance on smaller datasets. One promising solution lies in leveraging pre-trained models for data augmentation. Although such techniques have been successfully applied to computer vision, their NLP counterparts are less developed. We investigated two data augmentation methods for smaller NLP datasets using a previously successful cross-domain technique. Our experiments, conducted on three benchmark NLP tasks, demonstrate that these methods, namely retraining and score-based re-ranking, consistently outperform baseline data augmentation techniques. Moreover, our findings indicate that at least one of the proposed techniques generally yields superior results compared to standard data augmentation practices.

The Unified Gamma Function is redefined through the Hankel path and the reciprocal Gamma Function is subsequently defined based on this unified function. The storage properties of both are then proven. The series expansion of the unified gamma function can be expressed in terms of the gamma values at non-negative integers.

Top quark creation through hadron collisions is crucial in particle physics, particularly in the context of the Standard Model. Using the ATLAS detector and utilizing 36.1 $fb^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV, we have measured the semi-leptonic cross section for top quark pair production, specifically in the process where one top quark decays leptonically and its antipartner decays hadronically. To identify these events, we employ an matrix element method, taking into account the kinematics of the final state particles to reconstruct the top quark pair. The observed semi-leptonic cross section is measured to be 1.906 ± 0.055 (stat.) ± 0.075 (syst.) ± 0.045 (lumi.) $pb$, which is in line with the predicted value of perturbative quantum chromodynamics for top quark pair production via dilepton channels.

Our proposed framework is designed to handle tasks even when the database is empty, offering a robust method for execution that can be refined using actual database contents. To ensure stable performance under these conditions, we developed an instruction-aware loss function to guide the instruction encoder in learning generalizable semantic instructions. The encoder learns to capture the underlying semantic structure of instructions, making them less sensitive to specific object names. We also introduced a feature-aware loss function to adjust the encoder when the database is populated, ensuring the instructions maintain name-invariance while capturing relevant semantic information. The model's performance can also be optimized by adjusting the weighting between these loss functions based on whether the database is filled. Furthermore, we introduced a novel instruction re-ranking method to improve the model's performance by comparing the similarity of the top-ranked and second-to-top instruction features. This simple yet effective approach yields significant performance gains with minimal computational cost. Last but not least, we introduced an instruction diversity loss function to encourage the generation of diverse instructions for the same query, preventing the model from over-relying on a single, high-frequency instruction and enhancing its overall performance.

Machine learning on graphs is increasingly popular, but utilizing them while
preserving privacy presents significant challenges. Our novel framework, graph-
RDP, effectively computes privacy loss in DP learning on graphs of any structure,
from simple to highly complex. Building upon our theory, we successfully apply it
to various learning scenarios, including robust mean estimation and learning high
dimensional triangles. Our results demonstrate that the additional privacy loss
incurred by learning on graphs is often much smaller than previously estimated,
especially in common scenarios where the graph is sparse and has a low diameter.

The Euclid spacecraft, set to launch in 2022, will undertake a comprehensive mapping of the sky in the near-infrared and visible light spectrums. With its advanced capabilities, Euclid will be able to identify billions of galaxies and measure their distribution in space, as well as their gravitational lensing effects. This data will have profound implications for the fields of cosmology and cosmic structure formation, and will also enable research in a wide array of other areas, including exoplanets, the solar system, the Milky Way, stellar populations, and the universe at large. In this article, we explore the potential for Euclid to contribute to the field of X-ray astronomy, and discuss the various research topics that could be enabled with its data, such as the study of cosmic structure and the evolution of the universe.

Accurate lane keep systems (LKS) in autonomous vehicles are vital for basic navigation and overall safety. However, their performance can be compromised by even minor sensor errors. To thoroughly test LKS, this research develops a complex road network with an automated method for generating a variety of test scenarios, including Errant Object Placement (EOP) with uncertain object positions. By using the moment problem, we derive the probability distribution of object positions in the EOP test cases. Furthermore, we derive the probability of an automated vehicle colliding with the errant object, taking into account the uncertainty. This method and the generated test cases are publicly available for exploration at our GitHub repository. Our EA-RN road network generation method can produce complex N-shaped road configurations in under a minute, with a collision probability assessment of approximately 0.01 seconds.

Developing a personalized music playlist that aligns with a listener's mood and context relies heavily on music metadata, particularly audio content. Music audio content can reveal underlying patterns and features that traditional tags like genre or tempo may overlook, ultimately enhancing playlist quality. In this research, we explore the connection between music audio content and user listening behavior, focusing on how these elements influence a user's enjoyment of a playlist. To address this, we focus on extracting meaningful features from raw music audio, such as tempo, key, and genre, and investigate their impact on user preferences. Our proposed feature set, MUSICO, utilizes modern deep learning techniques to represent music audio content in a way that captures subtle similarities and differences between tracks, and we validate its effectiveness through a set of evaluation metrics and user studies.

A one-particle density matrix approach to hydrodynamics is being advanced to capture non-equilibrium quantum correlations, specifically focusing on linearized HSD.  We've developed a linearized scheme that incorporates fluctuations, based on the expansion of the Wigner function, which provides an efficient and computationally feasible method for simulating quantum correlations in HSD.  The proposed linearyzed scheme is being compared to QMD for validatory purposes, demonstrating superior accuracy in preserving quantum correlations.  The scheme is being applied to a model system consisting of two interacting plates, demonstrating its ability to accurately describe quantum correlations in a system with time-varying boundary conditions.  The research also explores the effects of model parameters on quantum entanglement, demonstrating the system's capacity to generate moderate quantum entanglement under specific conditions.

Action segment detection in video is a challenging task due to the difficulty in localizing temporal action regions amidst abundant background regions. To address this challenge, action segment detectors often rely on heavy two-stream networks, which are computationally expensive. To improve the efficiency of action proposal generation, we introduce the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), a lightweight yet effective network that leverages a cross-stream design to aggregate background context from both horizontal and depth dimensions. The DCAN utilizes stream-aggregation modules that integrate spatial and temporal features, achieving a compact structure with high efficiency. The proposed network enables action detection with a single-pass proposal generation, unlike traditional multi-stage methods. Our experiment results demonstrate the superiority of DCAN over state-of-the-art action detection benchmarks, and the code is available on GitHub.

A new approach has been developed to analyze bifurcations between magnetic islands and edge localized modes in plasma. The approach uses a bootstrap current model to create an extended neoclassical calculation for magnetic island growth and a reduced kinetic calculation for edge localized mode structure. It is based on an equilibrium optimization that balances these two components. By applying the method numerically, a connection has been demonstrated between magnetic island bifurcations and the formation of palm tree modes. The palm tree mode structure consists of an outer ELM-flux-row and an inner neoclassical-flux-row, separated by a small neoclassical island. The method's predictions for the small island size match observed values, while the small island's position can shift due to resistive coupling with the outer island.

A potential field method is a widely used and intuitive approach for creating local path-planning algorithms in robotics. Despite the issue of getting trapped in local minima, researchers have developed various modifications to potential field methods to enhance their effectiveness. This paper proposes using non-Euclidean geometry to create a novel potential field that incorporates repulsive vorticity, allowing for a more efficient avoidance of collisions between robots. The algorithm can identify multiple trapped minima and utilize the vorticity in the potential field to facilitate smooth navigation around other robots. Furthermore,VeCF can be viewed as an extension of the gradient vector field method, but unlike the original approach, it does not require the decomposition of potential field components. This new algorithm has been successfully implemented and its performance compared to the original method and other potential field-based methods in a practical scenario involving multiple robots.

The probability of a random letter sequence from an alphabet occurring more than expected in a renewal process with extremely long intervals can be quantified by a principle of quenched large deviation theory. This is possible provided the renewal process's tail distribution does not follow a power law. When the distribution's tail exponent is two or three and the letters are not equilikely, we can calculate the exponent of the corresponding LDP as the maximum letter frequency increases. This principle allows us to understand how rare events occur in systems governed by renewal processes and is an important consideration in the study of language and communication systems.

This paper investigates the potential of using intelligent reflecting surfaces to enhance the performance of radar that is not operating on a direct line-of-sight path. By analyzing the capabilities of non LOS-based radar, we derive the fundamental limits of range resolution and target velocity detection resolution, taking into consideration statistical properties of the radar signal, which is unique as it depends on both the direct line to the target and the reflected path from the surface. This analysis fills a gap in previous research that has primarily focused on LOS scenarios. Our findings reveal that refocusing the reflected power at the target can significantly improve range resolution by up to 3/2 times the wavelength, whereas increasing the power transmitted directly to the target has a less pronounced effect. Moreover, we examine how the surface can be configured to optimize the resolution of target velocity, and propose a low-complexity reflective method that can achieve near-optimal performance.

Using a pre-trained model as the starting point for continual learning is a common practice, yet multiple studies have demonstrated that doing so can result in negative transfer and hinder performance. This paradoxical issue of Pre-training being detrimental to subsequent learning tasks has led some researchers to suggest that training should be viewed as a form of continual learning. Building on this perspective, we developed a simple framework to resolve negative transfer in the context of NTL. Our method employs an optimal class weighting strategy to balance the training of new tasks with previously acquired knowledge. This framework is so effective that, in comparison, leading continual learning methods surpass Nearest Mean Classifier when using a pre-trained backbone. As a result, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art NTL solutions on three distinct task sets, without necessitating significant modifications to standard continual learning techniques such as replay-based or optimization-scenario approaches.

Building on earlier research by several authors, we establish a key property concerning maps from a space to a product involving a wedge sum. Specifically, given a space $X$, a point in $X$, topological groups $\pi_0\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{N}$, and a based space $A$ with a trivial second homotopy group, the only obstruction to maps from $X$ to $\mathcal{P}\wedge A\cdot \mathcal{N}$ that share the same first homotopy group as maps from $X$ to $\mathcal{P}\times A\times \mathcal{N}$ lies in a specific higher homotopy group. This finding fills a gap in earlier conjectures, allowing calculation of maps from $X$ to $\mathcal{P}\rtimes A\rtimes \mathcal{N}$ with specific first homotopy groups.

To investigate a one-dimensional domain's one-dimensional parabolic equation $u_t=u_{xx}+f(u)$, stability and instability of an equilibrium point directly impact the long-term behavior of its solution. Notably, when an unstable saddle focus is present at a given corner, there exists a stable manifold consisting of functions that determine the behavior of solutions within a specific, finite range. This study focuses on identifying this stable manifold as the image of an unstable focus's stable manifold through a diffeomorphism.

To gain a deeper understanding of the $n$ = 40 subshell gap's monopole component interaction, we employed the in-gamma technique to investigate the excitation pattern of 64Ni. By analyzing the average energy of particles observed in 63Cu following a gamma transition from an early state, we identified the two-state vector model (TSVM) as a suitable framework to analyze the observed data. By incorporating the effective interaction between the $p$3/2 and $f$5/2 neutron orbitals and the effective interaction between the $p$1/2 and $g$7/2 proton neutron cross terms, we utilized the TSVM to reconstruct the 63Cu low-lying state spectrum through the neutron and proton $s$-d shell configuration interaction model. Furthermore, based on the particle-rotor model, we analyzed how the $i$13/2 intrinsic orbital in 62Cu influences the 64Ni 0+2 state's energy. By integrating these factors, the subshell gap's energy can be effectively reconstructed within the $s$dfpng7/2 model space, and the 64Ni 0+2 state's energy can be explained within the np2sdp model space.

In our research, we extend the concept of Lipschitz games by allowing different players to have their own distinct Lipschitz values. This generalization is then applied to verify the existence of equilibrium strategies in games that cannot be classified as standard Lipschitz games.

We have developed a new model evaluation technique, J-K-fold CV, based on overlapping training and validation sets, as a more dependable alternative to standard K-fold CV. This was necessary due to the high variability in performance estimates from the data partitions used in model evaluation. J-K-Fold-CV was first proposed in a different context by J. S. Rosser in 1997. The method was hard to apply due to its complex resampling procedure, which involved solving an additional optimization problem for each validation set. We have now simplified the J-K-Fold-CV procedure, making it more feasible, with minimal impact on its performance estimates. This improved version was experimentally validated on artificial datasets, showing its reduced variance compared to standard K-Fold CV.

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning have achieved remarkable success in producing lightweight student networks that excel at image representation tasks, however utilizing deep teacher networks as guides for training these students has yielded limited gains. This study investigates two architecture types, including group-wise and channel-wise, and demonstrates that the success of teacher student methods relies heavily on the alignment of computation graphs between students and teachers. By introducing the UniNet framework, a unified architecture that is compatible with various teacher student methods, we achieve notable improvements in performance on multiple benchmark datasets. Furthermore, our work indicates that channel alignment is a more effective strategy for creating efficient student networks when using state-of-the-art self-supervised methods as training guides.

We have developed a comprehensive theoretical model that accurately describes light absorption in a system with high saturation levels, taking into account the impact of photon recoil. This model reveals the distinct behavior of lineshape in absorption, which reduces to a previously established first-order formula under low saturation conditions. The new understanding is applied to existing experiments involving nuclear spin precession in a gas, specifically the Hasegawa experiment with spin-3/2 particles and the Kim experiment with spin-1/2 neutrons. Both experiments exhibit lineshape features that provide insights into the current and future measurements of nuclear spin precession frequencies.

The study of static transitions in the space of configurations has a long history in the understanding of critical exponents and the universality of critical behavior in granular materials. Frictionless and frictional systems exhibit distinct behaviors with the former showing second-order dynamics and the latter showing first-order dynamics. A key limitation of previous studies was the absence of a comprehensive theoretical framework that could account for the full spectrum of ordering conditions and intermediate cases. A recent development in this field involved the identification of a unifying critical index $\lambda$ that describes the dynamics of the transition. In this study, we apply this index-based framework to validate the predicted behavior for both systems and discover that the critical indices for frictionless ($\lambda \approx 1.0$) and frictional shear jamming ($\lambda \approx 0.5$) indeed differ. A notable outcome of this study is the confirmation of Kurchan's hypothesis and the implication that materials near the point of rigidity have a reduced effective dimensionality.

The strength of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions can be adjusted by modifying the spin-orbit coupling strength, according to first-principles calculations. This is made possible through the use of a chiral exchange interaction that combines two Heisenberg exchange interactions with opposite signs. By fabricating a multilayer structure consisting of a thin metallic layer sandwiched between magnetic insulators, the DM interaction strength can be controlled. A theoretical model is then applied to a sample structure, and it is found that a slight change in the spin-orbit coupling strength can significantly increase the DM interaction strength, resulting in a shift from approximately 0.2 meAÅ to over 2 meAÅ. This level of control over the exchange interaction could enable dynamic management of magnetic properties in future devices.

The traditional approach to modeling WIMP-velectron scattering, which assumes a simple form for the incident WIMP momentum distribution, may not accurately reflect reality. A detailed examination of the incident halo WIMP momentum distribution reveals a significant inconsistency with the simplified model, particularly in the momentum range where electron scattering occurs. A new, more precise method for calculating the "effective" one-dimensional momentum distribution is now proposed and implemented, taking into account the three-dimensional nature of the WIMP momentum distribution and its orientation relative to the one-dimensional measurement. A mathematical formula for the effective distribution is derived and compared with full Monte Carlo simulations, showing a high degree of agreement. The implementation of this new method results in notable changes to the calculated scattering rates, especially in the low momentum range, where the differences between the traditional approach and the effective method can be as high as an order of magnitude. This has significant implications for the interpretation of potential electron scattering signals from direct detection experiments.

The proliferation of search engines has facilitated the dissemination of knowledge across public sectors, from government to education. However, indiscriminate reliance on search results can perpetuate discrimination due to inherent biases within these outputs. Although various factors influence search rankings, a significant concern is the bias stemming from the training data, which has been further exacerbated by the widespread adoption of machine learning techniques. While studies have previously assessed the biases present in Web data, there is a lack of research examining the propagation of these biases in search engine outputs. This study aims to investigate the biases present in Web data as reflected in search engine rankings, using public sector professionals in South Korea as the target audience. Through the analysis of their decision-making processes in relation to the search results, we found that the professional expertise of these individuals does not necessarily mitigate the discriminatory impact of the results. Moreover, the propagation of biases present in Web data was found to be pronounced in the search engine outputs. To validate these findings, controlled experiments were conducted to rule out alternative explanations, and the results also indicated that the bias present in the outcomes was influenced by the specific professional domain in question.

The proposed TeV-scale muon collider, with its distinct capabilities compared to the LHC and a future TeV-scale proton collider, with advanced polarized beams, could enable a wide range of particle physics investigations, from QCD and EW studies to dark matter and neutrino interactions. This includes the direct dark matter production via a neutrino portal mediated by a heavy Z' boson, which is particularly interesting given recent astrophysical and cosmological observations that could be explained by such a scenario. In this paper, we examine the feasibility of dark matter production at the muon collider for the U_B-L model, focusing on scenarios where the Z' mass is around 1-5 TeV. With a 10 TeV muon collider operating for 10 ab^{-1}, we find that the scenario is consistent with the local and Galactic center gamma-ray excesses, the 3.5 sigma neutrino excess, and the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon, without conflicting with other experimental data. Furthermore, we investigate the possibility of distinguishing the Z' from the SM weak bosons via a combined analysis of muon scattering processes and demonstrate the potential to precisely measure the dark matter coupling at the muon collider.

Compressed-sensing atomic sampling (rCASPR) is a newly developed technique 
that utilizes adaptive sampling to accelerate rotationally averaged contrast 
sensitivities in nuclear chemistry. In this study, we applied total-variation 
compressed sensing to enhance the advantages of rCASPR, allowing for a reduction 
in over-relaxation while maintaining high data efficiency. Our proposed method 
demonstrates a significant improvement over traditional linear sampling, featuring 
a narrower point-spread function and enhanced image contrast. Additionally, 
reduced variance was achieved through a novel area-based weight function, rCASPR-AW. 
We validated our approach using both simulated data and real-world experiments on 
nuclear chemistry measurements of the magnesium isotopes. The compressed-sensing 
rCASPR method has the potential to increase the efficiency of nuclear chemistry 
measurements by decreasing the required measurement time or the size of the ion 
beam necessary to complete a given experiment.

This paper introduces a novel concept called isotonic control barrier functions (ICCBFs) for both linear and non-linear systems. ICCBFs extend the ideas of Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and Higher Order Control Barrier Functions (HOCBFs) to work across a wider range of systems. Like CBFs and HOCBFs, ICCBFs provide sufficient conditions ensuring a system reaches a desired set in finite time while maintaining safety. The paper develops ICCBFs from first principles, presents computation methods, and provides verification techniques through both theoretical and practical examples, including a linear system, a non-linear spacecraft model, and a non-linear pendulum.

In this research, we extend our previous work on topological properties within CF-approximation spaces. Specifically, an RF function is defined to mimic the behavior of continuous functions on certain sets known as CF-closed sets. CF-closed sets represent a type of closed domain in CF-topology, an analogue of closed domains in traditional topological spaces. Our analysis of these sets has led to the identification of sufficient conditions under which the CF-topology of a CF-closed domain can be expressed as the restriction of the topologies of its constituent parts in a product space.

We introduce an innovative exact algorithm for the paired-permutation test that operates within a defined time frame. This algorithm leverages dynamic programming and achieves a solution within 2^k iterations for a sample size of 'k', effectively addressing 'k' up to 30 or 40 in practical scenarios. The paired-permutation test is widely employed to statistically evaluate data sets where random shuffling is not applicable. Despite its extensive usage, many researchers still rely on Monte Carlo simulations to approximate p-values due to the paired-permutation test p-value's combinatorial complexity. Our novel algorithm significantly outperforms Monte Carlo simulations in efficiency, providing an exact p-value with substantially fewer computations. As a result, it becomes feasible to calculate exact p-values for substantial data sets, encompassing up to 10^5 or more observations.

A significant shift occurred in 1983 with the breakdown of shipping cartels, leading to a notable change in the free market dynamics of the global oil industry. This study leverages a structural vector autoregressive (SVAR) model to analyze the effects of this transition on freight rates, shipping volumes, and oil prices over the long term. By applying vector error correction models (VECM) to data spanning from 1883 to 2013, our findings reveal a pattern where collusive behavior kept oil prices low and freight rates high, whereas the onset of a free market resulted in lower oil prices and reduced freight rates. A switch-and-regression model further validates these results by comparing the two distinct periods and highlighting a persistent relationship between freight rates, shipping volumes, and oil prices even after the breakdown of the cartel.

We have developed a novel concept of loom spaces, which extend topological vector spaces by incorporating additional structure, thus generalizing both fuzzy vector spaces and product fuzzy vector spaces. By integrating the ideas of both, loom spaces represent a novel framework that includes them as subsets. We have also introduced the notion of a loom cover and corresponding loom homology groups to further explore this new concept. Notably, every loom space can be broken down into a simple, explicit triangulation consisting of standard geometric shapes. This allows us to determine a key property of these spaces - they all possess a homology group equivalent to that of the ordinary space (i.e., it is zero for all positive integer values). Furthermore, we have identified conditions under which a loom space can be associated with a simple, explicit triangulation of another topological space (i.e., the torus).

Deep learning models for node classification in graph-structured data have made significant progress in recent years, primarily due to improvements in node attributes. Although graph connections are abundant, they are not as easily accessible since each edge is standardized. Despite graph connection data being more prevalent, it is not being utilized to its full potential. In an effort to better understand this issue, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of edge data, performing the first systematic evaluations of edge data on graph learning tasks. Our experiments revealed notable performance gains from edge data, outperforming improvements from node features, and demonstrated that current models do not effectively utilize edge data, leading to similar results across different data sets with varying attributes. To address this issue, we proposed simple yet effective augmentation techniques to prevent over-smoothing and over-readout, and found that our method achieved a substantial improvement of up to 15%.

A widespread issue in dimensionality reduction is the use of inappropriate pre-processing that can distort robustness. This problem of adaptive input has led to significant research on boosting-based pre-processing methods to enhance the robustness of various estimation methods and dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA and SVD. On the other hand, simply using traditional estimators without any pre-processing in a dimensionality reduction context results in better robustness. Building on this finding, our work investigates the feasibility of forgoing boosting-based pre-processing in favor of a direct application of traditional estimators in a dimensionality reduction context. Our theoretical analysis proves that both sparse PCA and SVD can be achieved with no pre-processing by simply applying traditional estimators. Furthermore, our findings are supported by extensive numerical experiments.

In theories describing superconducting behavior, particularly the Ginzburg-Landau theory, the fundamental distinction between a moving magnetic flux line and a localized vortex is not apparent. Through a mathematical analysis, we demonstrate that a moving flux line possesses greater entropy than a vortex in motion, a difference rooted in the presence of an extended magnetic field surrounding the flux line. By estimating this additional entropy based on the flux line's position relative to the vortex, we identify a region of about a coherence length around the vortex where the entropy is maximally increased by approximately half a flux quantum. Furthermore, we explore the implications of this entropy density on the interaction between vortices and flux lines, particularly in the context of vortex pinning.

This paper explores a novel approach to efficiently communicating and adjusting
aggregated power demands in a distributed system. We focus on a method of maximum
entropy feedback (MEF), enabling communication between an aggregator and system
operator without revealing individual user information. We analyze MEF's
effectiveness in a stochastic load system under a given utility function,
demonstrating its ability to represent the aggregated data accurately and assist
the system operator in optimizing global utility while safeguarding individual
user privacy. Through a case study of an energy aggregator, we show that MEF can
facilitate not only the exchange of load information but also enable the
aggregator to provide energy adjustment recommendations to the system operator.

This research develops a deep learning framework to anticipate stock movements,
which incorporates a component that can forecast technical indicators alongside
prices. By using a dataset of historical prices and technical indicators from
88 US stocks, results show that our proposed method can accurately predict the
direction of stock movements in the testing phase, outperforming a baseline model.

Type Ia supernovae can originate from white dwarf mergers, which can produce heavy elements up to iron through nuclear fusion. This study investigates the impact of such events on the isotopic composition of a specific type of meteorite, known as H chondrites, by focusing on molybdenum isotopes. Using a specialized model, researchers accounted for various factors, including contributions from different types of supernovae, neutron star mergers, and the processing of material by planetary bodies. Their findings revealed that white dwarf merger events play a significant role in establishing molybdenum isotopic composition, primarily due to their greater abundance compared to other processes. Furthermore, the study suggests that these events contribute a specific range of percentages to the global inventory of molybdenum isotopes.
