In general relativity, a new parameterization is proposed that could facilitate an analytical non-relativistic expansion. By defining a specific set of conditions, we demonstrate how general analytical expansions become possible. A key aspect of this proposal is showing that the standard weak-field expansion can be recast as just one instance of this pre-non-relativistic framework. Furthermore, a general formula is derived for the corresponding correction terms in the metric tensor.

We revisit the holographic computation of scalar field expectation values and potential energy in a setup where an asymptotically Anti-de Sitter space has a simple scalar field dependence on one coordinate. Using the principle of bulk locality, we demonstrate that the computation can be restructured as two separate differential equations, with only one involving the fundamental coordinate. This simplification is further applied to BPS giant graviton cases, allowing us to verify previously computed results for the vertices of these cases.

We investigated the motion of a horizontally moving cylinder within a granular material, specifically sand, in a narrow channel. We drove the cylinder at various rates and recorded the drag force it experienced, as well as the velocity of the channel walls. We observed that the drag force is not constant and fluctuates over time and space, with its magnitude depending on the driving rate, channel size, and properties of the sand. We also noted that the average drag force does not follow the linear response principle. At lower driving rates, a deep indentation forms in the leading edge of the channel, resulting in increased drag. In contrast, higher driving rates produce a shallower indentation, a flow pattern resembling a moving river, decreased drag, and decreased wall velocities. Furthermore, we found that the energy dissipated during the cylinder's motion is most efficiently used at higher driving rates.

We conducted an in-depth exploration of ionised gas outflows in star-forming disk galaxies using a comprehensive dataset from optical and X-ray observations. Our analysis focused on the impact of outflows on the depletion times of gas in these galaxies, which are forming stars at a high rate. By comparing the sizes of optical and X-ray components, we found evidence of gas outflows in 24 spectroscopic members of the Magellanic Clouds field. Our results show that outflows can extend up to ten times further than the optical regions of the galaxies, indicating that a significant amount of ionised gas escapes the galaxies' gravitational pull. This escaped gas contributes to a gas depletion times that is approximately 200% longer than what is suggested by a simple balance between neutral and ionised gas phases. The effects of outflows on gas depletion times are most pronounced in massive galaxies experiencing strong outflows, which suggests that these galaxies may be missing a significant amount of mass in the form of escaping gas. Our study provides the first observational constraints on the mass loss due to outflows in starbursting disk galaxies, which is an area that requires further investigation through more robust statistical analysis.

Finding the optimal configuration for a complex system is a challenging task,
especially when numerous parameters need to be adjusted simultaneously. This
problem is prevalent in various applications, including the development of
complex software systems. While auto-tuning is a common approach to system
configuration, existing methods often rely on predefined configurations and
strategies, limiting their effectiveness. In this work, we introduce BoAnon, an
innovative framework that utilizes anonymous auto-tuning to identify efficient
system configurations without relying on predefined settings. By integrating
Boolean Difference Cubing with cluster-based configuration learning, BoAnon
efficiently explores the configuration space by evaluating performance
differences between different subsets of program variants. We demonstrate
BoAnon's efficacy through its application to the configuration of the R* tree
software, achieving a significant improvement in query processing time
compared to the default configuration.

Our analysis of 2D non-plane flow coefficients in proton-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV reveals that the $p_T$ dependence of the $v_3$ coefficient behaves similarly for different particle types, much like the $p_T$ dependence of the $v_2$ coefficient. Furthermore, we found that the $v_3/n_3$ and $v_2/n_2$ ratios exhibit comparable $p_T$ dependencies across various particle types, including protons and pions in mid-rapidity. These observations are consistent with hydrodynamic predictions that incorporate a thermal $p_T$ spectrum.

Our research team at QualityAssurance for the Semantic Web has developed an innovative approach called DistQualityAssessment, which leverages sampling techniques to enhance the quality assessment of extensive RDF datasets. The goal of quality assessment is to identify and rectify errors within these datasets, but their size often makes this process computationally prohibitive. To overcome this challenge, our approach utilizes sampling methods to achieve accurate quality measurements at a fraction of the computational cost. Building upon our previous work on estimating quality with random sampling, our new algorithm refines this approach to produce more precise quality assessments. In contrast to the previous model, our new approach combines the strengths of the JUNO quality estimator with the sampling framework, resulting in more reliable results. Moreover, our approach can accommodate non-unique entities, a common scenario in the Semantic Web. Experimental evaluations on large datasets demonstrate that our approach delivers accurate quality measurements, surpassing the previous model and the JUMBO quality estimator while processing the entire dataset.

We develop a robust alternative to maximum likelihood estimation for independent increment and markov processes, called minimum density power divergence estimators. These estimators provide a reliable method for obtaining parametric estimates, and we prove their consistency and asymptotic normality. Our theoretical findings are supported by simulation experiments and real data analysis, demonstrating the estimator's effectiveness in process modeling.

Active galactic nuclei emit powerful shock waves that ionize surrounding gas through multiple mechanisms. These methods, including the conventional and two-mirror models, significantly affect the temperature and ionization state of the gas, ultimately influencing its emission characteristics. We developed two computational tools to visualize and estimate the emission properties of gas affected by single- and two-mirror shock models. These tools, ionize1d.py and ionize2d.py, can be found in our publicly available GitHub repository. We applied these tools to model the ionization structures created by shocks in active galaxies, taking into account various factors such as shock velocities, magnetic field strengths, and cooling times. We found that the two-mirror shock models predict observable features in the X-ray to radio wavelengths that could be explained by known phenomena in active galaxies. We also discovered that the models predict observable emission in the terahertz wavelengths, which could be used to test the models with upcoming telescopes. We also suggest that the the1d profiles predicted by the models could be testable with future spectroscopic observations.

IoT applications are increasingly prevalent, yet they are still plagued by numerous security vulnerabilities. Automated testing of these applications is essential for their safe deployment, but the complex testing landscape poses significant challenges. To facilitate testing, a framework called Frisbee has been developed, which utilizes test suites and a graph-based parsing method to streamline the testing process. Although Frisbee offers a practical testing solution, its effectiveness is hindered by its reliance on precise matching between tests and the application under scrutiny. This limitation can be rectified by integrating natural language processing into Frisbee, which would enable more flexible and robust test matching. By doing so, Frisbee can evolve into a more capable testing tool that is better equipped to handle the complexities of IoT applications.

Recent discoveries of rare $B$ meson decays, such as the $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$, $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$, and anomalies in $B$ meson decays to lepton pairs, present an exciting opportunity to conduct more thorough tests of the Standard Model and to explore potential hints of new physics. In this context, we perform a detailed analysis of rare $B$ meson decays within a specific beyond-Standard-Model framework - a two Higgs doublet model featuring one complex scalar doublet and one real scalar doubleat, coupled through a four-point interaction. Through an in-depth examination of the relevant decay processes within this model, particularly focusing on the effects of the real doublet's parameters on the decay rates and branching fractions, we find that the $B^0_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+\mu^-$ branching ratios are heavily influenced by penguin and box diagrams, with the former having a dominant impact. Furthermore, we calculate the $B^0_s-\bar{B}^0_s$ and $B^0-\bar{B}^0$ mixing parameters within this model and determine that the new physics contributions are negligible compared to the standard model predictions. By comparing our theoretical findings with experimental measurements and applying relevant constraints from electroweak precision data and the trilinear Higgs

A neural network-driven generative model can create realistic training data for traffic scenarios, potentially enhancing the accuracy of algorithms designed for autonomous vehicles. However, most such models struggle to generate high-quality scenes due to limited training data. In this study, we introduce SceneGen, an architectural framework that models complex multi-object traffic scenes by breaking down the problem into two components: predicting object attributes and arranging their spatial distribution. By using cross-modal feedback during this process, SceneArranger and SceneProp are able to refine the arrangement of generated objects, resulting in more accurate scenes that align with physical laws and the camera's perspective. Experiments show that SceneGen enhances the performance of several visual perception algorithms by up to 15% compared to using its generated data for training, including those that rely on LiDAR point clouds.

A key aspect of the Ising model on a Cayley tree is its connection to a nearest neighbour commutation relation for the discrete series group on that same tree. Employing the transfer matrix method derived from this representation, we successfully calculated both the partition function and the local magnetization for the Ising model within the tree. Furthermore, our calculations on the discrete series group on the Cayley tree allowed us to calculate both the local and global entropies for the system, as well as investigate the behavior of the mutual information between spins on different generations of the tree.

This article introduces a novel family of nested variants for the standard FGMRES iteration, designed to leverage preselected sets of numerically computed restrictions to reach a more accurate numerical solution. Under specific assumptions, we derive convergence properties for the proposed nested subroutines and observe enhanced performance through several illustrative examples.

This research extends previous discoveries made in [14] and addresses unresolved questions posed in [14]. Specifically, we consider a countably infinite grid of independent and identically distributed random variables, which serve as the sites of an exchangeable and regenerative map that imitates the behavior of a uniformly ergodic Markov chain with a finite state space. Our key discovery demonstrates the joint ergodicity of the exchangeable and regenerative map when considering a particular type of function that does not depend on the starting state, in addition to observing the absence of a central limit theorem for related functions, regardless of whether they depend on the starting state, all while assuming the distribution of random variables does not follow a uniform distribution. Furthermore, this finding can be applied to address several open problems posed in [14].

We investigate the evolution of dust within superbubbles, especially those containing a collapsing cloud core, using a multi-zone hydrodynamic model. This approach accounts for gas dynamics, energy dynamics, dust production and dynamics, and dust destruction processes, including radiative transfer. We specifically analyze the dynamics of dust in superbubbles, focusing on pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae, and specifically the formation of dust within massive molecular clouds. Our results show that pair-instability supernovae can create long-lasting dust tails, while core-collapse events can create long-lived dust tails when they occur before the cloud core collapses. Core-collapse dust can be recycled, with some of it falling back into the cloud core. Dust tails can be replenished by subsequent supernovae, with core-collapse dust surviving longer than shell dust. Our findings also indicate that core-collapse dust can contribute significantly to the overall dust budget of superbubbles, with up to 50% of the dust mass being contained within the cloud core. This dust can contribute to the overall dust budget of superbubbles, with up to 50% of the dust mass being contained within the cloud core. This can contribute to the observed dust in nearby galaxies.

This research addresses the challenge of 3D object detection in far fields by
leveraging both RGB and lidar data. In scenarios where lidar can determine
position but not identity, we propose a detection method that fuses these
sources. Specifically, we suggest using a pre-trained object recognition model
to classify objects based on RGB data and then adjusting the corresponding 3D
bounding boxes with adjustments based on the object's rotation and size,
thereby linking their visual and depth information. We present an efficient
implementation of this process by modifying the attention mechanism in a
single-stage 3D detection model to perform object recognition. Experimental
results on the KITTI dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and
show significant gains in far-field detection accuracy when compared to using
only a lidar-based detector.

Utilizing machine learning to create quantum states within chemistry is called Quantum Monte- Carlo (QMC) based quantum neural network (QNN) or generative modeling. We present an efficient method for the automatic differentiation of the Fermionic Neural Network (fNN) QNN model, which is a widely used and accurate approach. This new technique outperforms existing methods by a factor of ten in computation speed, which is important for practical applications due to the large number of parameters in fNN QNNs. We demonstrate its effectiveness by successfully preparing ground and excited states of molecular systems like H2 and N2.

During surgery, the registration of organ models to a patient model using flexible models can be compromised by measurement noise present in intraoperative data. A Bayesian approach is presented here that treats organ shape and stiffness as random variables, allowing for the estimation of their distributions given imperfect data. A finite element method is employed to model organ physics, while the dimensionality reduction technique known as Proper Generalized Decomposition (PGD) accelerates the approach. The algorithm is based on maximizing a probability function that incorporates physical laws and statistical assumptions, with an additive regularizer used to stabilize the result. The proposed method is fast due to PGD, and it is shown here that this approach effectively mitigates the impact of noise present in intraoperative data through both numerical simulations and an experimental study using MRI images.

Building upon previous research, this paper extends earlier results to a wider class of materials, specifically those whose energy-momentum tensors exhibit degeneracy. It demonstrates that for such substances, only the most basic conformal symmetries can exist, and these can be further understood in terms of their associated geometric properties. A key finding is that if a degenerate material has a specific type of collineation, it necessarily has a non-zero scalar field and its energy-momentum tensor can be expressed in a particular form related to its degeneracy.

Self-supervised methods for flow estimation have made significant advancements,
yet accurately predicting occlusions remains a challenge in current approaches.
Most existing techniques treat the occlusion map as an additional target to be
learned, but we argue that the flow and the occlusion are intrinsically linked and
cannot be easily treated as separate objectives.
To address this limitation, we propose a novel method that treats the occlusion not
as a pixel-wise mask, but as the displacement field of the foreground object
segmentation.
This approach inherently models the occlusion without the need for additional
supervision or explicit occlusion learning.
To make this concept feasible, we introduce a multi-task network that simultaneously
optimizes the flow and the object segmentation.
Our method's simplicity and effectiveness have been demonstrated through
comprehensive evaluations on standard datasets.

This research introduces a novel network called a Temporal Sparse Resonating
Network (TSRN) as a versatile classifier capable of handling both binary and
multi-class tasks. The proposed model is designed to outperform conventional
artificial neural networks (ANNs) in terms of processing speed and power
consumption. The algorithm of the proposed network is based on a simplified
version of the Hopfield model, focusing on the generation of stable states
within a set of interconnected neurons. The research also presents an approach
to construct the network's connection matrix using a gradient descent method, which
can be easily parallelized. The proposed algorithm is tested and shown to
effectively compete with the performance of conventional multi-layer perceptrons
(MLPs) on both synthetic and real-world data sets.

This research investigates the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter under the influence of a strong external magnetic field, and we calculate the corresponding masses of spin-polarized strange quark matter massless EOSs in various ranges of the magnetic field strength, and and the results are then used to construct an EOS table for two-polarization, spin-polarized, and unpolarized strange quark matter.

A cubic graph is classified as even-2-factorable, or E2F for short, if it can be decomposed into multiple 2-factors with even lengths. It has been established that subdivided Tait graphs are always C4F. This study aims to identify the conditions under which a graph can be classified as E2F through 2-factor augmentation, a process involving the addition of edges to an existing even-length 2-factor. A necessary and sufficient condition has been established to determine when a graph can be classified as E2F through 2-factor augmentation. This condition has been applied to analyze the 2-factor augmentability of non-C4F subdivided Tait graphs.

Using the Bateman-Horn Conjecture proposed by Li, this paper leverages the Borel-Cantelli Lemma to derive both an upper bound and a lower bound (under specific conditions) for the frequency with which the quadratic polynomials $ax^2+bx+c$ produce prime values as $a$, $b$, and $c$ vary within specified finite sets of natural numbers. Notably, if the natural numbers are allowed to vary without restriction, only an estimate of the growth rate of the sequence of natural numbers yielding the maximum number of prime values from $ax^2+bx+c$ can be obtained via the Borel-Cantelli Lemma and the classic Hardy-Littlewood "k-tuple" Conjecture. As a result, the exact growth rate remains uncertain. Furthermore, this paper obtains refined estimates for both cases, including a more precise estimate of $O\left(\frac{\log\log\log D}{\log\log D}\right)$ for a related growth rate in its main theorem.

Recent research has shown that system call rewriting can protect nearly all programs,
but it's typically limited to those written in compiled languages. For interpreted
applications written in PHP, Python, and similar languages, we introduce Timeloops,
a wrapper that enables precise system call extraction from program loops. By detecting
and eliminating infinite loops, Timeloops can then feed extracted system calls to
an application, allowing for efficient security protection. We demonstrate that
Timeloops offers robust security without sacrificing performance, outdating the
original programs by an order of magnitude in terms of overhead. Furthermore,
we show that it can safeguard a wide range of applications, from commonly used tools
like WordPress and Apache Solr to custom PHP services, and even malicious scripts.

A new scalar field, which may be a pseudo-Goldstone boson linked to a spontaneously broken global symmetry in a dark sector, is being investigated as a possible dark matter candidate. This investigation requires the introduction of several new terms in the effective Lagrangian, as the symmetry is not automatically preserved by general transformations. Consequently, the interaction between the dark matter and baryon number carrying fields necessates a U(1) symmetry that is simultaneously a global symmetry of the dark sector and an accidental symmetry of the SM. The nature of the pseudo-Goldstone boson significantly impacts the elastic scattering of dark matter with nucleons, with coherent scattering patterns resulting from equal charges under the baryon number carrying U(1) symmetry, and inelastic scattering resulting from opposite charges. Observations from direct and indirect detection, along with the decretion curve, provide constraints on the parameters of the model, which in turn, offer insights into the possible mass and decay constant ranges for the scalar sector.

This study develops an undirected multi-target tracking algorithm that can handle varying sensor detection ranges and different target identities. An innovative approach is introduced to tackle the challenge of detecting absent targets within each time period. A directed graph is used to organize joint assignments and an innovative cutoff rule is proposed to significantly reduce the computational demands by limiting assignments and preventing unnecessary subdivisions. Our algorithm's performance is compared to other methods using both simulated data and real-world footage. The results show our approach not only provides more accurate target tracks but also experiences lower processing times.

This research modifies a previous study on controllability for a semilinear population dynamics equation that doesn't allow for degenerate diffusion. We demonstrate that an observability inequality derived from the previous work can effectively manage total extinction of the population within a specified timeframe, achieved by introducing a source term that follows the maximum principle and doesn't force immediate extinction at any point in time or space.

This study proposes a next-generation goal-scoring AI for soccer, utilizing a simulated environment to train an AI agent that can attempt goal scores from a distance of 30 meters. The AI is trained in a simulated soccer game where the sole objective is to score goals, bypassing any need to tackle, pass, or shoot from a distance. The environment is designed to award the highest possible reward for goal scores and a significantly lower reward for other actions, thus making it difficult for the AI to learn any other strategy. Interestingly, the AI agent was found to be easily defeated by a human player who can only control one side of the game, and in some cases, the AI was even able to score multiple goals in a row. The researchers also found that the AI's performance could be improved by training it in 2D before moving to 3D, and that the additional complexity of 3D motion did not necessarily result in a significant improvement in performance. The code and simulated soccer game used in this study are available on GitHub.

A new approach to the Wilson-Garcon method for wave equation approximations is proposed, involving the use of time-domain wavefields in full waveform inversion. This subgradient method leverages adjoint-state wavefields in the compressed domain to calculate gradients, resulting in an efficient and accurate method. Theoretical justification for the method's convergence is provided, and its performance is validated through synthetic and real data experiments.

We present a quantum network theory that allows for precise control over the flow of information between two impurities interacting with a common photonic loop. By leveraging an interresonator coupling that distinguishes between left and right circular polarizations, we can manipulate the direction and efficiency of information transfer. This technique enables the creation of highly directional and chiral components, such as opto-isolators, quasi-circulators, and diodes with near 100% performance. Notably, this network can facilitate a phenomenon where information appears to teleport instantaneously from one end to the other, a result made possible by the unique properties of chiral resonators.

We have conducted an in-depth investigation of the IGR J19294+1816 source during its 2016-2019 high-intensity phase using the Insight-HXMT space telescope.  Our analysis revealed a complex spectrum that can only be accurately described with multiple components.  The primary feature observed was a high-energy spectral component with a temperature exceeding 100 keV, which is a rare characteristic among X-ray dim isolated blue compact objects.  The secondary component, a high-density Comptonization spectrum with a temperature below 30 keV, provides information about the compact object's mass that is more than one times the mass of the sun.  The combination of these two components also indicates that the compact object is likely a neutron star.  The third component, a partial absorption component, was found to be responsible for an increase in the overall hydrogen ionized gas density along the line of sight.  The estimated gas density is approximately 1.5 times 10 to the power of 18 per cubic centimeter.  The presence of this high gas density along the line of sight may be a key factor in the 2019 outburst of IGR J19294+1816.

Our analysis of the asymmetric noisy voter model in a two species competition reveals multiple potential results, including species dominance, coexistence, intermittent dominance, and random model dynamics due to noise-induced fluctuations. By studying a two-component system without spatial structure, we discovered either species can dominate, coexistence, or intermittent dominance based on the relative noise levels and relative attraction forces between species. A key factor in these models is the asymmetry between who influences whom in opinion changes. Our research shows that in some cases, intermittent dominance is more likely than in others, and that sufficient asymmetry leads to inevitable coexistence or specific forms of dominance.

Citizen science has the potential to significantly contribute to the documentation and study of Indonesian sundials. This form of participatory research can provide valuable historical data through photo collections and other contributions. Citizen science can also aid in the preservation of sundials by encouraging their conservation. However, there are challenges to implementing this approach, as some contributors may have misconceptions about the cultural significance of sundials, and others may have difficulties in accurately recording the information they provide. To address these issues, it is crucial to establish clear guidelines and incentives for contributors, as well as to offer user-friendly tools for data submission. Ultimately, citizen science can be a powerful approach to documenting and preserving Indonesian sundials, but it requires careful planning and execution.

This paper investigates the optimal design of a dual-function data and energy delivery system, where a base station transmits signals to both a data-receiving user and an energy-harvesting device alongside a power supply. In this system, the base station can either access two separate, risk-free transmission channels or utilize a power line that introduces random noise interference. Researchers analyzed three distinct transmission schemes, with a focus on two of them, by formulating a joint data and power transfer optimization problem to maximize the end-to-end transfer rate. Through the application of successive convex approximation techniques, optimal formulations were developed and characterized, with explicit expressions for key variables such as transfer delays, energy harvest amounts, and HAR fractions. Furthermore, a scheme transformation approach was established to demonstrate the ability to achieve near-optimal transfer rates in risk-free transmission scenarios. Numerical results validate the effectiveness of proposed methods and highlight the energy-harvesting system's ability to outperform traditional systems in terms of transfer rates.

The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated a shift to telework and the remote operation of experimental setups, accelerating the adoption of automated experimental methods. These methods involve combining data acquisition software with generative models like neural networks to formulate hypotheses, generate predictions, and determine optimal next steps to test them. While existing frameworks can accomplish this to some extent, they often lack the flexibility to create the same level of autonomy across various software and hardware configurations. This study introduces an open-source, modular, and reusable platform that accelerates the automation of complex, intricate experiments across multiple settings. Our speedup technique leverages a graph-based representation of the experimental process, allowing for the seamless integration of new components and the efficient management of intricate workflows. As evidence of its efficacy, we showcase our ability to replicate the XENON1T neutrino detection and mountain crab experiment, both of which are highly sophisticated, manually operated setups. Furthermore, we demonstrate the seamless creation of a telework-capable version of the mountain crab experiment.

A versatile, customizable electrostatic phase plate design is presented, featuring an intricate pattern of nanometer-scale openings that can be adjusted to varying degrees, allowing for fine-tuning of electron probe dimensions and current density distribution. The plate's design parameters, including opening size and arrangement, directly influence electron distribution and can be optimized to achieve desired outcomes, such as enhanced central current density or minimal central diffraction and spread. The plate's material, chosen to withstand high temperatures and resist heating, is crucial in determining its effectiveness and longevity. The design's effectiveness is demonstrated through finite element simulations and experimental validation, showcasing its potential to provide precise control over electron probes in scanning applications.

Pretrained language models have significantly advanced the field of dialogue understanding, and prior studies have primarily focused on evaluating various transformer-based approaches. In this research, we assess the performance of recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures in the field of dialogue understanding, which to our knowledge has not been previously done. We utilized long short-term memory (LSTM) and transformer-enhanced RNN (TENER) models, which incorporate previous dialogue history through textual and structural means. By employing a set of zero-shot and few-shot fine-tuned baseline methods across three datasets, we found that our RNN-based approaches consistently outperformed the baseline methods and comparable transformer-based models in terms of F1 score, particularly in the zero-shot and few-shot settings. We believe this work serves as a valuable reference for future investigations into evaluating RNN-based approaches in the field of dialogue understanding.

Understanding loop closures in varying environments using monocular images is a challenging task for vision systems. To tackle this, we propose a deep learning network that uses a Attention mechanism to focus on salient visual cues in images, enabling loop closure detection across changing environments. We experiment with multiple attention modules and evaluate their effectiveness, ultimately selecting the best-performing one. Additionally, we conduct a large-scale simulation to test the system's robustness to significant scale and location discrepancies, as well as varying image speeds. The results demonstrate that our proposed network, along with the selected attention module, can reliably detect loop closures in diverse scenarios. The system's performance is further enhanced by simulating varying camera speeds, loop closure detection rates improve as speeds increase.

YouTube's popularity as a streaming platform is largely due to its cloud infrastructure, which ensures a seamless user experience. Cloud services are capable of delivering high-quality video to end-users, and by leveraging the flexibility of streaming, YouTube can optimize its delivery by adjusting the number of cloud servers based on user demand. However, a sudden surge in demand can lead to a stream quality degradation. To mitigate this issue, YouTube employs a stream control mechanism that adds a margin to the number of servers required, a method that, while effective, can be conservative. In this study, we develop a dynamic stream control mechanism that utilizes a predictive model to forecast user demand and adjusts the stream quality in real-time, balancing the quality of the stream with the number of cloud servers in use. Our approach is validated through a cloud simulation, demonstrating the ability to provide a seamless user experience and optimize the number of servers required.

We investigate the temperature dependence of a doped graphene sheet's thermal properties, specifically focusing on its carrier density and half-filled band state. By employing a first-order adiabatic expansion in relation to a momentum space metric, derived from the random phase approximation, we analyze the impact of the renormalized quasiparticle velocity on the velocity and calculate the temperature-dependent renormalization of the chemical potential for a doped graphene sample. By the first order in the expansion, we find the temperature dependence of specific heat in a half-filled graphene sheet is directly proportional to the temperature squared.

Recent advances in text-to-speech synthesis using deep learning have produced high-quality, natural and expressive speech. Nevertheless, controlling the level of expressiveness in synthesized speech remains a challenge. To address this, we introduce MaskedSpeech, a novel text-to-speech synthesis system that overcomes this difficulty. By incorporating a control mask into the text encoder, MaskedSpeech learns to synthesize both natural and expressive speech. It can also interpolate between these two extremes to achieve desired levels of expressiveness. To evaluate the synthesized speech, we conducted a subjective assessment and found that MaskedSpeech outperforms existing methods in naturalness, controllability and expressiveness. Additionally, we demonstrate the system's ability to mimic the vocal characteristics of target speakers and control the expressiveness of synthesized voices.

We examine a solitary wave system in a one-dimensional setting, characterized by an anharmonic oscillator and a long-range interaction, described by a combination of the polynomial oscillator and the Laplace kernel in a scalar field theory. Exact numerical methods reveal that when the interaction is not quadratic, these waves lose stability, eventually disintegrating due to energy loss, with a rate influenced by the kinetic energy and the inverse of the kinetic to potential energy ratio. This research was conducted following the observation of solitary waves in a scalar field system with an atypical interaction and a one-dimensional lattice, discovering that while these waves are stable in this configuration, they become unstable in two-dimensional space.

The study of theories with multiple stabilizing symmetries is undertaken, and a scenario is identified in which a scalar field breaks two discrete symmetries while maintaining a third. A fourth state is found that can achieve stability by breaking only the last symmetry, and at energy scales much lower than the original, leading to the formation of a Q-ball. The difference in energy between two configurations of the field, where one breaks all three symmetries and the other only the last, is found to be minimal, and it is directly related to the shape of the potential and the ratio of mass scales. A range of models is proposed to illustrate the general findings, and their common characteristic is a multi-valley structure.

Our study investigates a specific model of a cyclic universe, excluding a Big Crunch singularity, driven by holographic dark energy. This model is analyzed through the lens of the holographic principle, using two approaches to the UV cutoff: one associated with the entire universe and another with the universe's horizon at any given time. We assess the universe's entropy across the cycle, considering the volume of a d-dimensional manifold that matches the number of degrees of freedom in the volume. The impact of the Granda-Oliveros cutoff parameter on the model's behavior is evaluated through graphical analysis, with two distinct results obtained for the two approaches to the UV cutoff. A significant cutoff dependence is evident when the universe's volume is considered, whereas the irrotational energy density displays minimal cutoff dependence in the ecocentric approach. We also explore the possibility of a stable limit cycle, assessing the relationship between the energy density of the contracting and expanding phases. Contrary to expectations, a stable limit cycle is found in the ecocentric approach under specific conditions, which may offer a pathway to reconcile the apparent horizon volume law with the cosmological observations.

This informal note is meant to convey the essence of the research by J.-M. Lozano and A. Soldevila, which examines certain highly ramified extensions related to specific Galois groups added to the rational numbers.

The search for invisible decays of the Higgs boson can be significantly affected by the nature of neutral long-lived particles (LLPs). If these particles have varying decay lengths, no single search strategy is universally effective. To address this, a combined approach using multiple LLP detectors and thorough background modeling is necessary. This paper explores a particular scenario, where a scalar LLP decays invisibly into dark matter, linked to the mediator that produces it. With several LLP production mechanisms considered, we perform a search across the fermion LLP parameter space using a Monte Carlo model. This model is then compared with current experimental data from the CMS and ATLAS collaborations, across the full range of the ATLAS electric dipole moment search. Ultimately, this study emphasizes the importance of a tailored, data-driven approach to background estimation for each LLP detector.

Recent studies on word meaning changes often overlook a critical aspect: the shifting dynamics of language use over time. This phenomenon can be quantified through a model that accounts for individual word usage variations and is supported by extensive datasets. Our analysis of three large corpora, spanning from 1990 to 2019, reveals the complex interplay of factors that contribute to perceived shifts in language. This interplay is best understood by examining the relationship between changes in contextual dynamics and time. As a consequence, some words may seem to undergo a temporal evolution in meaning, while others remain static, all within the framework of a universal pattern of change.

We establish stringent limits on ultra-light scalar and axial particles with a mass below 1 eV, utilizing the well-characterized properties of warm dark matter. Our analysis utilizes the observed smoothness of the cosmic microwave background and the suppression of power at large scales in the dark matter power spectrum to derive these constraints. The effective field theory of inflation is utilized to account for the production of these particles during the reheating phase, with the outcome depending on the particle's mass, the temperature at the end of the reheating period, and the temperature dependence of the effective number of relativistic degrees of freedom, or $N_{\rm eff}$. In the three-field model, the constraints are further refined by considering the relationship between the maximum temperature of the universe and the inflation energy scale. The produced ultra-light particles are found to constitute less than a certain percentage of dark matter, with the corresponding particle density constraints falling within a certain range, with the most restrictive bound occurring at a certain particle mass. The constraints derived in this study are more stringent than those obtained from the Milky Way's phase-space distribution, the fermionization of WIMP candidates, stellar dynamics, the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, and the Bullet Cluster observation.

While the structural development of the retina is well-documented, a comprehensive understanding of nuclear migration dynamics during retinogenesis is still lacking. A computational model was employed to analyze the relationship between nuclear distribution within retinal layers and the migration dynamics during retinogenesis in this study. A dimensionless parameter was derived from a multi-layer growth model, reflecting both nuclear distribution and the dynamics of nuclear migration. A dataset was created using a mouse retina wholemount staining technique, and a nuclear distribution function was fitted to the data. After extracting feature values from the fitted function, these were compared with a timecourse dataset obtained from a mouse retina growth simulation. A strong correlation was found between nuclear distribution and a composite variable consisting of the inverse of the outer retina thickness multiplied by the sum of the extracellular pressure and a tension-related variable. A similar relationship was found experimentally in a mouse retina. Furthermore, a more intricate model was found necessary to explain the distinct migration pattern within the retinal ISL layer. Both a numerical and an analytical solution to this model were developed. As a result, it was discovered that the model can be simplified to a one-dimensional problem under certain conditions. However, one condition of this simplification is not met in the ISL layer, leading to a more complex nuclear distribution. This complexity is reflected in a bi-phasic pattern of nuclear packing within the ISL layer.

In image recovery from incomplete data, a widely used method is mutual coherence-based optimization. However, its high computational cost has limited its practical applications. A more efficient alternative is to employ O1-norm minimution for coherent sensing matrices, a approach particularly effective for recovering missing data in structured images. For incompressible signals, a novel mutual low-coherence factor (MLCF) is proposed, which balances mutual coherence and sparsity. An alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm is then developed to solve the MLCF factorization problem. This factor can be incorporated into recovery models with RANSAC to handle outliers, or with Laplacian regularization for incomplete data. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of computational efficiency and reconstruction quality.

We investigate the dynamic scaling properties of active matter systems in dimensions
between 2 and 5, questioning the applicability of linearized hydrodynamics in this range.
Through Monte Carlo simulations, we analyze an orientation order model suitable for all
these dimensions and collect empirical evidence that points to significant deviations
from hydrodynamic predictions in this intermediate dimension range. To test the
alternative hypothesis of anomalous scaling, we develop a simplified model that can be
used for dimensional analysis between 1D and higher dimensions and perform Monte Carlo
simulations to compare with the main model. Our results indicate that the intermediate
dimension range may indeed be anomalous and that the dimension $d=4$ serves as the
critical point for the 'repulsive' version of the model.

This research aims to offer a comprehensive overview of email security issues affecting academic research institutions globally. It offers an in-depth examination of vulnerabilities exploited through common email threats, along with the techniques used, their impacts, and real-world examples. Furthermore, it discusses email protection measures, along with the strengths and weaknesses of current security software. Finally, the study proposes directions for future research in email security.

van Hove singularity in the cuprate material $\mathrm{La}_{2-x}\mathrm{Sr}_x\mathrm{CuO}_4$ has been
analyzed to determine its characteristics and implications. By analyzing the
transition's characteristics, a consensus on the corresponding $x$ value was
reached, which in turn has significant implications for the transition's
associated properties. The determined $x$ value has been used to predict the
behavior of the cuprate system at that doping level, which exhibits optimal

by the presence of charge order. Moreover, the EX-VH transition's implications
